Derivatives behind a prediction's standard errors

Source: R/predict-jacobian.R
hzr_jacobian.Rd

Experimental. Returns the Jacobian that predict.hazard() used for the standard errors of a se.fit = TRUE result, row for row with the result as you hold it now: after selecting, reordering or repeating its rows. With it, any weighted sum of the predictions has a delta-method standard error, such as the expected number of events in a cohort, which is the sum of the cumulative hazards at each patient's own time.

Usage

hzr_jacobian(object)

Arguments

object

A data frame returned by predict.hazard() with se.fit = TRUE, possibly with its rows selected, reordered or repeated.

Value

A list with three elements: J, a matrix with one row per row of object and one column per parameter, holding the derivative of that row's fit with respect to the parameter; vcov, the covariance matrix of those parameters; and names, the parameters' names as summary.hazard() names its coefficient rows. For weights w, the standard error of sum(w * object$fit) is sqrt(t(g) %*% vcov %*% g) with g = colSums(w * J).

Details

The derivatives are stored on the result when predict.hazard() returns it. R keeps that stored copy unchanged when you select or bind rows, so it can describe rows the result no longer has, or miss rows it now has. This function matches each row of object to the row of the prediction it came from, by its row name (a repeated row, named "2.1" by [, matches row "2"), and checks that its fit and se.fit are exactly the values that row was given. It stops, naming the first row it cannot match, rather than return derivatives for the wrong rows. Results bound together from more than one call to predict(), or whose fit or se.fit columns were changed or rounded, are refused: compute their derivatives from each original result and combine the pieces by names.

The columns are the parameters the standard errors used. A parameter held fixed in the fit without a variance, or one the prediction does not depend on (such as a coefficient whose covariate is 0 in every row), is left out, so two predictions can have different columns. A Weibull fit's first column is log(mu), not mu.

See also

predict.hazard()

Examples

set.seed(1)
dat <- data.frame(time = rexp(60, 0.3), status = rbinom(60, 1, 0.7),
                  age = rnorm(60))
fit <- hazard(survival::Surv(time, status) ~ age, data = dat,
              dist = "weibull", theta = c(0.3, 1, 0), fit = TRUE)
# Each patient's cumulative hazard at their own follow-up time.
res <- predict(fit, newdata = dat, type = "cumulative_hazard",
               se.fit = TRUE)
j <- hzr_jacobian(res)
g <- colSums(j$J)
c(expected = sum(res$fit), se = sqrt(drop(t(g) %*% j$vcov %*% g)))
#>  expected        se 
#> 47.000008  6.855655
